title: The Square Deal
subtitle: The White House, 1901–1909
intro: He arrived by assassination at forty-two and treated the office as a place to act from rather than preside over. Trusts broken, a coal strike settled, a canal begun, a war ended, and a fleet sent round the world. Fifteen questions on eight years.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt gave the Executive Mansion the name it still carries. What was it?
questions.explanation: People had called it the White House informally for decades, but Roosevelt made it official in October 1901, putting the name on his stationery. It was a small act that said something larger about how he meant to occupy the place.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his private office
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: Which railroad combination did Roosevelt's government break up, establishing him as a trust buster?
questions.explanation: Northern Securities, a holding company assembled by J. P. Morgan, E. H. Harriman and James J. Hill to combine the great northwestern railroads. Roosevelt had it prosecuted under the Sherman Act in 1902 and the Supreme Court ordered it dissolved in 1904. Wall Street was genuinely shocked that a president would do it.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt at work in his office
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: In 1902 Roosevelt intervened in a major strike. Which industry?
questions.explanation: The anthracite coalfields of eastern Pennsylvania. Around 147,000 miners had walked out in May, and with winter coming the country faced a fuel crisis. Roosevelt summoned both sides to the White House in October and pressed them into arbitration — the first time a president had intervened in a labour dispute as something other than a strike-breaker. The precedents ran the other way: the Homestead lockout of 1892 ended with Pinkertons and the state militia, and Cleveland sent the regular army against the Pullman strikers in 1894. The commission Roosevelt appointed gave the miners a shorter day and a wage rise and left their union unrecognised — fair treatment all round and no more than fair, which is roughly what he meant by a square deal.
questions.imageAlt: A 1904 campaign poster with portraits of Theodore Roosevelt and Charles W. Fairbanks
questions.credit: For President, Theodore Roosevelt; For Vice President, Charles W. Fairbanks, 1904. Lithograph by Louis Roesch Co., San Francisco. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt call his domestic programme?
questions.explanation: The Square Deal — the promise that capital, labour and the public would each get fair treatment and no more than fair treatment. The New Nationalism came later, in 1910, after he had left office.
questions.imageAlt: A 1904 campaign poster with portraits of Theodore Roosevelt and Charles W. Fairbanks
questions.credit: For President, Theodore Roosevelt; For Vice President, Charles W. Fairbanks, 1904. Lithograph by Louis Roesch Co., San Francisco. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906. For what?
options: Mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War
Beginning construction of the Panama Canal
Settling the Venezuelan boundary dispute with Britain in 1895
questions.explanation: For brokering the peace between Russia and Japan. He was the first American to win any Nobel Prize, and the first sitting head of state anywhere to win it. He kept neither the medal's cash nor the credit for long: the money went to a fund for industrial peace rather than into his own account, and the treaty he had forced on the two delegations was so unpopular in Tokyo that crowds rioted in Hibiya Park when its terms were published.
questions.imageAlt: The Nobel Peace Prize certificate awarded to Theodore Roosevelt
questions.credit: Certificate of the Nobel Prize. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where were the Russo-Japanese peace talks held?
questions.explanation: Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in the summer of 1905, chosen partly because it was cool in August and had the communications a major diplomatic event required. The resulting agreement is still known as the Treaty of Portsmouth.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt's Nobel Peace Prize certificate
questions.credit: Certificate of the Nobel Prize. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did the United States obtain the right to build a canal across Panama?
options: By purchasing the isthmus outright from Colombia for $40 million
Under the Clayton–Bulwer Treaty signed with Britain in 1850
By treaty with Colombia, ratified in Bogotá in 1903
By treaty with Panama weeks after it broke from Colombia
questions.explanation: The Hay–Herrán Treaty of January 1903 would have bought the strip from Colombia, and the American Senate approved it — but Colombia's senate rejected the terms that August. Panamanian separatists declared independence on 3 November, the USS Nashville sat offshore, the United States recognised the new republic within days, and the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty was signed on 18 November by a Frenchman acting as Panama's envoy. The $40 million went not to Colombia but to the bankrupt French canal company for its concession and equipment; Panama got $10 million. The Clayton–Bulwer Treaty had actually forbidden the United States exclusive control of any such canal, which is why it had to be superseded first. It remains the most criticised episode of his presidency, and he never apologised for it.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt addressing canal workers at Bas Obispo, Culebra Cut
questions.credit: Panama Canal. Pres. Roosevelt at Bas Obispo, Culebra Cut, addressing the workers. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt travelled to Panama in 1906 and did something no sitting president had done before. What?
options: Left the country while in office
questions.explanation: He became the first sitting president to leave the United States. He went to see the canal being dug, climbed into a ninety-five-ton Bucyrus steam shovel for the photographers, and made sure the picture got home.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt operating an American steam shovel at the Culebra Cut, Panama
questions.credit: President Roosevelt running an American steam-shovel at Culebra Cut, Panama. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: Which two landmark consumer-protection laws did Roosevelt sign in 1906?
options: The Federal Reserve and Federal Trade Commission Acts
The Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act
questions.explanation: Both in 1906, and both owing something to the public revulsion that followed Upton Sinclair's The Jungle. Sinclair had aimed at the conditions of the workers and hit the nation's stomach instead — as he put it himself.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: In October 1901 Roosevelt caused a national furore by doing what?
options: Dining with Booker T. Washington at the White House
Pardoning the anarchist who had shot President McKinley
Refusing to move into the Executive Mansion at all
Appointing the first woman to serve in a president's cabinet
questions.explanation: Washington came to dinner on 16 October 1901, six weeks into the presidency — the first time a president had entertained a Black American at the White House as a guest rather than as a caller on business. The Southern press ran editorials for weeks and one senator's response was violent enough that it is still quoted as a marker of the era. Roosevelt later wrote that he had not devoted much thought to the matter beforehand; he never repeated the invitation, and the two men met afterwards on Washington's ground at Tuskegee rather than his own.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt and Booker T. Washington at Tuskegee Institute
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt and Booker T. Washington at Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was the Great White Fleet?
options: The dredging fleet that cut the Culebra Cut
Sixteen battleships sent around the world
A programme of subsidies for American merchant shipping
The white-hulled steamers of the Great Lakes grain trade
questions.explanation: Sixteen battleships with their hulls painted peacetime white, sent on a circumnavigation that left Hampton Roads in December 1907 and came home in February 1909, two weeks before Roosevelt left office. He sent them partly to impress Japan, partly to prove the navy could coal and supply itself that far from home, and partly to make it politically impossible for Congress to shrink the fleet afterwards. When the Senate threatened to withhold the money he pointed out that he already had enough to get the fleet to the Pacific, and Congress could decide whether to pay for the trip back.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt aboard the Mayflower reviewing the fleet at Hampton Roads
questions.credit: President Roosevelt reviewing the fleet from the Mayflower, Hampton Roads, Virginia, 1907. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's approach to foreign policy is usually summarised by which phrase?
options: Speak softly and carry a big stick
questions.explanation: He used the line publicly as vice president in 1901 and attributed it to a West African proverb. The point people usually miss is the first half: the softness of the speech was supposed to be doing as much work as the size of the stick.
questions.imageAlt: The Great White Fleet returning from its world cruise to Hampton Roads
questions.credit: "Welcome home!" The Great White Fleet returning from its world cruise. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In 1904 Roosevelt won the presidency in his own right. What did he announce on election night?
options: That he would not accept another nomination
That he would resign within two years
That he would seek a third term
That he would appoint his opponent to the cabinet
questions.explanation: He declared that having served three and a half years of McKinley's term plus a full term of his own, he would regard that as two terms and would not accept another nomination. He kept to it in 1908 and regretted it almost immediately — which is why he ran again in 1912.
questions.imageAlt: A 1904 campaign poster with portraits of Theodore Roosevelt and Charles W. Fairbanks
questions.credit: For President, Theodore Roosevelt; For Vice President, Charles W. Fairbanks, 1904. Lithograph by Louis Roesch Co., San Francisco. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt used a word for journalists who exposed corruption — one that stuck, though he meant it as criticism. What was it?
questions.explanation: Muckrakers, borrowed from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress — the man with the muck-rake who could look no way but downward. Roosevelt used it in 1906 to warn that relentless exposure without hope could corrode public life. The journalists took the name as a badge of honour.

questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: Who succeeded Roosevelt as president in 1909?
questions.explanation: William Howard Taft, his Secretary of War and personal choice, whom he pushed to the nomination and then left to it while he sailed for Africa. Within three years the friendship had collapsed and Roosevelt was running against him.
